summary: Describes the RTP payload format of the Secure Communication Interoperability Protocol (SCIP), an application-layer protocol for end-to-end session setup, payload encryption, media packetization, and reliable transport. It serves as a public reference for equipment and procurement.

eli5.summary: Secure phone calls need an agreed way of packing sound into internet packets. This explains the packing used by SCIP.

subtitle: How encrypted SCIP secure voice and video rides inside RTP, and why the network should treat it as an opaque clear channel.

tldr.problem: SCIP is an application-layer secure communication protocol whose specification is not public. Network equipment that does not recognize SCIP in an SDP declaration may strip it out, and SCIP endpoints then fail to work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes SCIP's RTP payload as an opaque, encrypted stream. It defines the audio/scip and video/scip media subtypes and the SDP mapping, and it tells network devices to relay the traffic unchanged, like Clearmode.
tldr.outcome: Network vendors and administrators get a public reference so they can allow SCIP and leave its payload alone. The IESG notes that the IETF could not review the non-public SCIP-210 specification and cannot verify its security claims.

facts.label: Encrypted by SCIP
facts.value: RTP payload only, not the RTP header or RTCP

facts.label: Network handling
facts.value: Must not modify SCIP RTP packets

today: RFC 9607 is a Proposed Standard from July 2024 and has not been obsoleted or updated. The SCIP protocol itself is defined in SCIP-210, which the RFC says continues to evolve independently of this document.

sections.title: What the Document Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9607 describes the RTP payload format of the Secure Communication Interoperability Protocol (SCIP). SCIP is an application-layer protocol that provides end-to-end session establishment, payload encryption, packetization and de-packetization of media, and reliable transport. It uses RTP as a basic transport and is registered as the audio/scip and video/scip pseudo-codecs.

The RFC is a globally available reference for people who build network equipment or buy services that must carry SCIP. The key points are that SCIP needs only a basic RTP channel, comparable to Clearmode in RFC 4040, that it does not require SRTP, and that middleboxes should not try to parse the payload.

The IESG Note says this specification depends on SCIP-210, which is not publicly available. The IETF could not conduct a security review of it, so it cannot verify any of the security claims in the document.
sections.eli5: This explains how a secret phone or video call is packed into internet packets. It also asks the networks in the middle to just pass the packets along.

sections.title: Background and the Problem for Networks
sections.content:
SCIP began in the United States as the Future Narrowband Digital Terminal (FNBDT) Protocol in the late 1990s. A group of U.S. Department of Defense and vendor members, the Interoperability Control Working Group, managed it. It later grew to include NATO, NATO partners and European vendors, and the group was eventually renamed the SCIP Working Group. NATO adopted SCIP in STANAG 5068. First-generation devices ran on circuit-switched networks, and SCIP was then extended to radio and IP networks.

The difficulty is that SCIP standards are available mainly to government and military communities and selected equipment makers. Network vendors and administrators may therefore not know about the scip media subtype. Some network devices do not recognize SCIP and may remove it from the SDP media payload declaration. The RFC states that SCIP endpoint devices do not operate on networks if the subtype is removed.

Registering the subtype and describing it publicly gives equipment makers a common reference to recognize SCIP and lets administrators write a security policy that permits audio/scip and video/scip.
sections.eli5: Some post offices threw away boxes they had never seen before. This RFC shows them what the box looks like so they let it through.

sections.title: The Payload: Opaque and Untouched
sections.content:
An RTP packet carrying SCIP is just an RTP header followed by a SCIP payload. The payload consists of encrypted SCIP control messages and codec data, and its size and interval vary a great deal with the state of the SCIP protocol. The network MUST NOT perform transcoding, lossy compression or other modification of it, and the streams MUST be relayed transparently as clear-channel data, like Clearmode.

SCIP has no upper-layer syntax of its own, such as NAL units. It encrypts the output of the audio and video codecs it uses (the RFC gives G.729D and H.264 as examples) after that output has been formatted for RTP as usual. The SCIP application layer makes sure everything sent to RTP fits within the MTU. The receiving side handles identification, ordering and reassembly, and the SCIP layer handles error detection and retransmission when needed.

Because SCIP will keep evolving, network devices MUST NOT filter SCIP RTP traffic based on what is currently observed or documented, and they MUST NOT modify SCIP RTP packets. Any change is detected as an integrity violation by the endpoints, leading to retransmission and eventually communication failure.
sections.eli5: The contents are locked in a sealed box that only the two ends can open. Anyone in the middle who tampers with the box just breaks the call, so they should leave it alone.

sections.title: RTP Header Fields and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RTP header fields SHALL conform to RFC 3550. SCIP traffic may be continuous or discontinuous, and a session is likely to contain both. For discontinuous transmission the Timestamp field MUST increment based on the sampling clock. For continuous transmission it depends on the sampling rate of the underlying media. The Marker bit SHALL be zero for discontinuous traffic, and for continuous traffic it follows the underlying media subtype.

For congestion control, the bitrate can be adjusted according to the capability of the underlying codec (the RFC names MELPe and G.729D), and the number of encoded audio frames per packet can also be adjusted. Applications using RTP over UDP SHOULD implement their own congestion control and MAY implement a transport circuit breaker. The AVPF and SAVPF packet loss feedback mechanisms are OPTIONAL, because SCIP itself manages retransmission of some errored or lost packets.

Extra RTP tools that do not modify the SCIP payload are optional and left to the vendor. The RFC lists generic forward error correction, multiplexing RTP and RTCP on a single port, symmetric RTP and BUNDLE as examples.
sections.eli5: The outside of the envelope follows the usual post office rules. If the road gets crowded, the sender can send smaller or fewer letters at a time.

sections.title: Media Subtypes and SDP Mapping
sections.content:
The payload format is identified by the scip media subtype. A clock rate of 8000 Hz SHALL be used for audio/scip, and 90000 Hz SHALL be used for video/scip. Both registrations list no required or optional parameters, are binary, and are only defined for transfer via RTP, with no transcoding as the stream crosses the network. The published specification is SCIP-210 and the change controller is the SCIP Working Group.

In SDP, the media type goes in the m= line, and the subtype and clock rate go in a=rtpmap. The optional ptime and maxptime attributes map to a=ptime and a=maxptime.

SCIP has its own capability exchange. SDP offer/answer therefore only needs to negotiate the use of SCIP itself, and the codecs carried inside it are negotiated through SCIP control messages. A device SHALL list the SCIP payload type in order of preference on the m= line.
sections.eli5: The label on the box says what kind of thing it is and how fast it ticks. What is inside is agreed later between the two ends.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The usual RTP security considerations apply, and the RFC says it is not a payload format's job to mandate how RTP is secured. Applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong security mechanisms.

The payload format does not impose uneven processing cost on receivers and has no active content, so it does not inherently create a denial-of-service threat from pathological data.

SCIP only encrypts the RTP payload. It does not protect the RTP header or RTCP packets. Applications that need that protection might consider SRTP, but the RFC treats such additional mechanisms as OPTIONAL. The IETF has not reviewed the security of SCIP itself and has not verified the claims in the document.
sections.eli5: Only what is inside the box is locked. The writing on the outside of the box can still be read, so add more protection if that matters.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The audio/scip and video/scip media subtypes were already registered in the Media Types registry. IANA updated those registrations to point to this document.

Section 8 gives contact details for the SCIP Working Group, which maintains SCIP and from which the current SCIP-210 specification may be requested. It notes that an older public version of SCIP-210 exists.
sections.eli5: The names for these two kinds of box were already in the official list. The list entries now point to this RFC.
